title: Do Hardwood Floors Increase Home Value in Seattle? What Appraisers and Buyers Say
meta: Hardwood floors raise Seattle home value, but appraisers and buyers reward them differently. Wills Flooring shows how it works and what installation costs.

blocks.lead: Yes. Hardwood floors increase home value in Seattle, but an appraiser folds them into a condition and quality rating rather than adding a line item, while buyers pay for them directly through faster sales and stronger offers.
blocks.detail: Wills Flooring installs engineered or solid hardwood for $3.25 per sq ft of labor, with material quoted separately. On a typical 1,000 sq ft Seattle main floor, that labor is a small share of what the floor returns at sale.

blocks.html: The question comes up in two versions. A Ballard owner planning to sell in two years asks whether new hardwood will show up in the appraisal. A Queen Anne owner who just bought asks whether the carpet-to-hardwood project pays for itself. Appraisers and buyers are two different audiences, and hardwood lands differently with each. This post explains both, with Seattle examples and the real installation math from our hardwood flooring price list.

blocks.text: How a Seattle appraiser actually treats hardwood

items.title: Comps, not receipts
items.text: A Seattle residential appraisal is built on the sales comparison approach: three to six recent sales of similar homes nearby. Your floors do not get a dollar line. They influence which comps get picked and how the appraiser adjusts between them.

items.title: Condition and quality ratings
items.text: Lender appraisals rate condition from C1 (new) to C6 (major repairs) and quality from Q1 to Q6. Worn carpet can push a home to C4. New hardwood on the main level often supports C3 and a stronger quality read, which moves the adjustments against comps.

items.title: What they photograph
items.text: Appraisers photograph the main living areas and note flooring type in the report. Hardwood in the living room, dining room and hall reads as a finish upgrade. Hardwood in a back bedroom nobody photographs contributes less.

items.title: Neighborhood expectations
items.text: In Wallingford, Green Lake and Capitol Hill, hardwood is the norm in comparable sales, so having it keeps you level with the comps and lacking it invites a downward adjustment. Where comps still carry carpet, hardwood is a modest upward adjustment.

blocks.note: Appraisers rarely credit the full project cost, but the condition rating can decide whether the appraisal comes in at contract price.

blocks.text: What Seattle buyers do that appraisers never will

items.html: They filter listings by photos. Buyers scrolling on a phone decide in seconds. A continuous hardwood main floor photographs as one bright space. Carpet in the living room reads as a project, and some buyers never book the showing.
They price the project into the offer, and then some. A buyer who sees 1,000 sq ft of tired carpet deducts what they imagine a floor costs, plus a hassle premium for weeks of living in a job site.

They move faster. Seattle agents tell us homes with refinished or new hardwood on the main level draw more first-weekend traffic. More traffic means competing offers, which is where the value actually shows up.
They read the inspection differently. An inspector who lifts a carpet corner and finds stained subfloor writes it up. New hardwood over a checked subfloor gives them nothing to flag.

blocks.text: When hardwood will not add value, or will add less than you spent

a.title: It pays when
items: The main living areas are carpet, laminate or worn sheet vinyl
Comparable sales in your Seattle neighborhood already show hardwood
You will live with the floor for a few years before selling
The subfloor is sound and the job fits the 500 sq ft minimum

b.title: It disappoints when
items: There is already original hardwood under the carpet that could be refinished
You are installing exotic species or wide plank far above the block's price tier
The kitchen and baths are dated and will absorb the buyer's attention instead
The floor goes into a basement or a room with a known moisture problem

blocks.title: Check under the carpet before you buy new wood:
blocks.text: Roughly half of the pre-1960 Seattle homes we visit still have original fir or oak beneath the carpet. Sanding and finishing that floor costs $3.99 per sq ft all-in and gets the same appraisal and buyer response as new hardwood. We lift a corner and tell you what you have before quoting anything.
How to make sure the value shows up at closing

items.html: Run one floor through the connected rooms. Continuous hardwood from the entry through the living and dining areas is what buyers and appraisers both register. Patchwork by room reads as partial work.
Pick a neutral, mid-tone or light color. Natural white oak, light stains and warm browns sell to the widest Seattle audience. Very dark or very red floors narrow the buyer pool.
Keep the paperwork. Give your agent the invoice, the material spec and our 1-year workmanship warranty. Agents use it in listing remarks and appraisers note documented upgrades.
Install a few months before listing. The floor is worth the same on day one, but a finished, lived-in home photographs better than one that smells like a job site.
Get the whole quote in writing. Labor, material, removal and subfloor prep should each be a line. Our price list is published so you can check the labor number before we arrive.

faq.q: How much value do hardwood floors add to a house in Seattle?
faq.a: There is no fixed dollar figure because appraisers adjust against comparable sales rather than adding a line for floors. National remodeling surveys have found new wood floors recovering roughly their full cost at resale, and in Seattle's hardwood-heavy neighborhoods the effect on buyer interest is usually stronger than the appraisal effect.

faq.q: Do appraisers give credit for new hardwood floors?
faq.a: Indirectly. Hardwood improves the condition and quality ratings on the appraisal form and can change which comparable sales are used. It does not appear as a separate dollar credit. The biggest appraisal benefit is avoiding a downward adjustment when every comp already has hardwood.

faq.q: Is engineered hardwood as good as solid for resale value?
faq.a: In Seattle, yes. Buyers and appraisers treat both as hardwood. Engineered is often the better choice in condos and over concrete, and Wills Flooring installs either for the same $3.25 per sq ft labor rate. A thick wear layer that can be refinished later protects long-term value.

faq.q: Should I install hardwood or refinish what is under my carpet?
faq.a: If there is sound original hardwood under the carpet, refinish it. At $3.99 per sq ft all-in it costs less than new wood and buyers love an original floor. We check what is there at the free estimate before recommending either option.

faq.q: Which rooms should get hardwood for the best return?
faq.a: Entry, living room, dining room, hallway and kitchen, in that order. These are the rooms that appear in listing photos and appraisal photos. Bedrooms add comfort but far less resale value, and bathrooms and laundry rooms are better served by vinyl plank.
